claims.text: A physics-informed surrogate ML model using multimodal microstructural descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed predictions will be within 20–30% of experimental values.
The proposed surrogate will be approximately ten times faster than full-scale simulations.
The reported hierarchical-heterostructured state of HfNbTiVAl10 has been characterized by synchrotron X-ray imaging.
Phase-fraction distributions, interfacial areas, and gradient lengths can be quantitatively extracted from high-resolution synchrotron imaging of this alloy.
Sub-micron synchrotron imaging and complementary imaging modalities are sufficient to capture the relevant hierarchical heterostructure.
Phase fraction, interfacial area, and gradient length mediate the relationship between microscale chemical fluctuations or phase boundaries and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Physically meaningful microstructural descriptors can improve or accelerate the learning of ML models.
The descriptor-based surrogate can capture stress localization, yielding, and crack initiation.
The surrogate can reduce reliance on high-fidelity atomistic or multiscale finite-element calculations.
Periodic recalibration with new experimental data ensures adaptability to shifts in microstructural descriptor space.
First-principles, molecular-dynamics, CALPHAD, and full finite-element approaches have significantly higher computational costs than the proposed surrogate.
Traditional approaches generally attain 10–15% accuracy improvements.
The method remains reliable when samples lie within the calibrated microstructural descriptor space.
Unrepresented phases, second phases, or atypical interface geometries can cause loss of predictive reliability.
Early benchmarks show notable gains in both efficiency and accuracy.
Model performance depends on image quality, descriptor comprehensiveness, and the representativeness of the calibration dataset.
Predictions deviating by more than 30% from independent measurements would falsify the stated accuracy hypothesis.
